newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Clinton shows relaxed style at APEC.
newsitem.headline: Clinton shows relaxed style at APEC.

text.p: Relaxed and smiling, President Bill Clinton mingled easily with the leaders of the Pacific Rim on Monday, displaying a confidence he once lacked on the world stage, aides said.
They said the president had grown in stature in his four years in office and credited him with steering this year's APEC gathering in Subic Bay towards endorsing U.S. objectives.

In their end-of-summit declaration, leaders of the 18-member Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum called on the World Trade Organisation (WTO) to "eliminate substantially" tariffs imposed on computers and telecommunications equipment by the year 2000.

The document was stronger than a statement drawn up by trade and foreign ministers of the APEC governments on Saturday, but still short of the original American goal of an endorsement for "zero tariffs".
Aides said Clinton had grown into his role as a world leader -- a task he found daunting when he first assumed the presidency nearly four years ago.
"He's developed a personal relationship with so many of the leaders," said a senior U.S. official who participated in many of the formal and informal talks Clinton had in the Philippines.
When Clinton entered the White House after 12 years as governor of Arkansas, he was cautious on the diplomatic front -- preferring to concentrate on domestic issues.

His first trip to Asia as president, in July 1993, was to the annual gathering of the leaders of the seven major industrial nations in Tokyo. He was tentative as the junior member of that group, and offered few ideas.
With his re-election now behind him, Clinton appears to be more confident on the world stage.
His 12-day trip to the Asia-Pacific region, which included a five-day stay in Australia and ends on Tuesday after a state visit to Thailand, has emphasised active U.S. commitment to the region.
Monday's summit followed bilateral talks between Clinton and China's President Jiang Zemin, Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto and South Korean President Kim Young-sam.

"Given the president's four years worth of relationship building in this region...there's a lot of trust in his ability to bring things along and bring things to a conclusion," said another high-ranking official.
